props.title: The Train
props.initialSlug: WW2 art heist pits Nazis against French resistance

sections.content: The Train (1964) stands as one of cinema's greatest resistance thrillers, with John Frankenheimer directing Burt Lancaster in a masterclass of practical action filmmaking. The film's premise - French Resistance fighters trying to prevent Nazis from stealing priceless art treasures by train - spawned countless imitators, including Monuments Men (2014) and Where Eagles Dare (1968). What sets The Train apart is Frankenheimer's insistence on practical effects - real trains were crashed, actual locomotives were destroyed. Lancaster performed his own stunts, bringing authenticity to every frame. The film's influence extends to modern action classics like Mission: Impossible (1996), where practical stunts ground impossible scenarios in reality.

sections.content: The film's technical achievements remain staggering. Frankenheimer rejected miniatures, insisting on full-scale train sequences that influenced everything from The Taking of Pelham One Two Three (1974) to Unstoppable (2010). The black-and-white cinematography by Jean Tournier and Walter Wottitz creates a documentary-like immediacy that later inspired Schindler's List (1993) and The Pianist (2002) in their approach to World War II drama. SUBHEAD: The Art of Resistance Cinema

While The Train excels as an action thriller, it's also a profound meditation on art's value during wartime, a theme later explored in The Monuments Men (2014) and Woman in Gold (2015). Paul Scofield's Colonel von Waldheim represents the Nazi obsession with cultural theft, while Lancaster's railway inspector Labiche embodies resistance through practical action rather than intellectual appreciation. This tension between art and survival would later influence films like The Rape of Europa (2006) and Francofonia (2015).
